To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the coastal GIS is evolving towards a more integrated approach to coastal management and that this approach is being influenced by the WSSD and the Millennium Development Goals.

(i) coastal GIS has evolved from an information management tool to a decision support tool, with the potential to become a knowledge-based tool, and (ii) coastal GIS will be most effective when it is used to address the ontological, semiotic, and hermeneutic arenas.

the role of GIS in integrated coastal management is changing as a consequence of: (i) changing approaches in coastal management, and (ii) changing approaches in the use of indicators in coastal management.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of GIS and its representations in the production of signifieds.
the evolution of GIS as an enabling tool for coastal management, and with how GIS may help to address some of the key issues of coastal sustainability.
the development of a conceptual framework for coastal GIS that can accommodate a multi-faceted approach to the production and use of coastal GIS in the context of the evolving international agenda.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
GIS has a key role to play in the implementation of the UN Millennium Goals, and the WSSD Plan of Implementation.
the role of coastal GIS is changing and will continue to change in response to a changing world.
coastal GIS has an important and growing role to play in the implementation of sustainable development.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the role of coastal GIS has evolved from the use of coastal GIS as a tool for decision support, through its use as a tool for integrated coastal management, to its use as a framework to facilitate a holistic understanding of the coastal zone.
the role of coastal GIS is evolving towards a more holistic, multi-faceted, and multi-dimensional one.
coastal GIS is not just a tool but a way of looking at coastal issues and of dealing with the coastal arena.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the role of coastal GIS has to be understood in a much broader context than just the technical aspects of data collection and analysis.

GIS is a powerful tool for coastal management and planning but its full potential can only be realized when the tool is used in a way that is consistent with the evolving nature of the coastal zone and the needs of the people who live in and depend upon it.
the coastal GIS community must continue to develop its own unique identity and approach to the challenges of the 21st century, rather than simply follow the lead of other disciplines.
